Worked Example 1

Job satisfaction can be influenced by many factors, such as salary and age. In our previous examples, we have already examined these variables based on a smaller, hypothetical database. Since multivariate linear regression works best on a larger database, let’s examine this relationship on a larger, 30-person database as well. We will perform the calculations using the jamovi statistical program again.

Step 1. Import database

Open the lin_reg_03.xlsx file in jamovi.

Step 2. Measurment levels

Check the measurement levels of the variables in the dataset. Set the measurement levels of the variables as follows: age, salary and job satisfaction as continuous variables.

Step 3. Scatter plot 1.

Create a scatter plot of the relationship between age and job satisfaction. Click on the Analysis tab and select Exploration / Scatterplot.

Step 4. Scatter plot 2.

Create a scatter plot of the relationship between salary and job satisfaction.

Step 5. Multiple Linear Regression

Perform a multivariate linear regression analysis with job satisfaction as the dependent variable and age and salary as the independent variables.

Interpretation of the Jamovi Linear Regression Output

This output shows the results of a multiple linear regression analysis conducted in Jamovi. Below, We will explain each section of the output and its meaning.

1. Model Specification

  • Dependent Variable: job_satisfaction

    • This is the variable we are trying to predict.

  • Covariates (Predictors): salary, age

    • These are the independent variables used to explain variations in job satisfaction.

2. Model Fit Measures Table

  • R (Multiple Correlation Coefficient = 0.98)

    • This indicates a very strong positive relationship between the predictors (salary and age) and the dependent variable (job_satisfaction).

  • R² (Coefficient of Determination = 0.95)

    • 95% of the variance in job satisfaction is explained by salary and age.

    • This suggests a very good fit of the model.

How to interpret R²?

  • Closer to 1 → Better model fit.

  • Closer to 0 → The predictors do not explain much of the variability in job satisfaction.

  • 0.95 is very high, meaning the model explains most of the variability in job satisfaction.

3. Model Coefficients Table

3.1. Interpreting the Coefficients

  • Intercept (β₀ = 8.14, p = 0.0192)

    • This represents the expected value of job_satisfaction when both salary and age are zero.

    • Since a salary of 0 and age of 0 are not realistic, the intercept itself is usually not of primary interest.

  • Salary (β₁ = 0.44, p < 0.0001)

    • Interpretation: For each additional unit increase in salary, job satisfaction increases by 0.44 units, holding age constant.

    • p-value < 0.0001, meaning this effect is highly statistically significant.

  • Age (β₂ = 0.53, p < 0.0001)

    • Interpretation: For each additional year of age, job satisfaction increases by 0.53 units, holding salary constant.

    • Again, the p-value is extremely low (< 0.0001), meaning the effect is highly significant.

3.2. Standard Error (SE)

  • Standard errors measure the uncertainty of the coefficient estimates.

  • Smaller SE values indicate more precise estimates.

  • Here, both salary and age have low standard errors, suggesting reliable estimates.

3.3. t-values

  • The t-statistic tests whether each predictor has a significant impact on job_satisfaction.

  • Higher absolute values indicate stronger effects.

  • All t-values (2.49, 19.13, and 7.49) are large, suggesting strong relationships.

3.4. p-values (Statistical Significance)

  • p < 0.05 means the predictor is statistically significant.

  • Here, both salary and age are highly significant predictors of job satisfaction (p < 0.0001).

Predicting

If interested in predicting job satisfaction for specific salary and age values, use the regression equation:

\[\hat{Y} = 8.14 + 0.44(\text{salary}) + 0.53(\text{age})\]

Final Interpretation & Conclusion

  • The model fits the data well (R² = 0.95, very high).

  • Both salary and age significantly predict job satisfaction.

  • For each increase in salary and age, job satisfaction increases significantly.

  • The low p-values (<0.0001) indicate that these relationships are highly statistically significant.

  • The model can be used to predict job satisfaction based on salary and age.

Step 6. Standardized Coefficients

The standardized coefficients are useful for comparing the relative importance of predictors. Click on the Model Coefficients bar and select Standardized estimate.

Interpretation of the Standardized Estimate Column in Jamovi

The standardized estimate column in the regression output provides beta coefficients ($\beta$), which allow for a direct comparison of the relative importance of different predictors in the model.

Definition of Standardized Estimate (Beta Coefficient)

  • The standardized estimate (also called the beta coefficient or standardized regression coefficient) measures the effect of an independent variable on the dependent variable in standard deviation units.

  • It removes the influence of different measurement scales by converting all variables to a standardized scale (mean = 0, standard deviation = 1).

  • Formula: \[\beta = b \times \left(\frac{\sigma_X}{\sigma_Y}\right)\] where:

    • \(b\) = unstandardized regression coefficient

    • \(\sigma_X\) = standard deviation of the predictor

    • \(\sigma_Y\) = standard deviation of the dependent variable

Interpreting the Standardized Estimates in This Output

Predictor Unstandardized Estimate (b) Standardized Estimate (β) Interpretation
Salary 0.44 0.83 Salary has the strongest impact on job satisfaction. A one standard deviation increase in salary leads to a 0.83 standard deviation increase in job satisfaction.
Age 0.53 0.33 Age has a weaker effect compared to salary. A one standard deviation increase in age leads to a 0.33 standard deviation increase in job satisfaction.

Key Insights:

  • The higher the standardized coefficient, the greater the relative importance of that predictor in determining the dependent variable.

  • Here, salary (β = 0.83) has a much stronger effect on job satisfaction than age (β = 0.33).

When to Use Standardized vs. Unstandardized Coefficients?

Coefficient Type When to Use? Interpretation
Unstandardized Estimate (b) When variables have the same unit of measurement (e.g., salary in dollars) Shows the raw effect (e.g., “$1 increase in salary raises job satisfaction by 0.44 points”).
Standardized Estimate (β) When variables have different measurement scales Allows for direct comparison between predictors to see which has the strongest effect.

Conclusion

  • Salary (β = 0.83) is the most influential predictor of job satisfaction.

  • Age (β = 0.33) has an effect but is less impactful than salary.

  • Standardized coefficients are useful when comparing the relative importance of predictors in the model.

Step 7. Model fit

Check the model fit statistics. Click on the Model Fit bar and select all options.

Interpretation of Model Fit Measures in Jamovi Regression Output

The model fit measures in the Jamovi regression output help assess how well the regression model explains the dependent variable. Below is a detailed explanation of each metric shown in the output.

1. Model Fit Measures Table

Metric Value Interpretation
R (Multiple Correlation Coefficient) 0.98 Indicates a strong relationship between the predictors (salary and age) and the dependent variable (job_satisfaction).
R² (Coefficient of Determination) 0.95 95% of the variation in job satisfaction is explained by the independent variables.
Adjusted R² 0.95 Adjusted for the number of predictors; confirms the model generalizes well without overfitting.
AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) 166.66 Used for model comparison; lower AIC means a better model fit.
BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) 172.27 Similar to AIC but penalizes model complexity more. Lower BIC is better.
RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) 3.41 The average prediction error in the same units as job_satisfaction. Lower RMSE means better predictive accuracy.

Interpretation of Each Fit Measure:

1. R (Multiple Correlation Coefficient) = 0.98

  • Definition: Measures the overall strength of the relationship between the independent variables (salary and age) and the dependent variable (job_satisfaction).

  • Range: 0 to 1

    • Close to 1 → Strong correlation.

    • Close to 0 → Weak correlation.

  • Here: R = 0.98, indicating a very strong relationship between the predictors and job satisfaction.

2. R² (Coefficient of Determination) = 0.95

  • Definition: The proportion of variance in job_satisfaction explained by salary and age.

  • Interpretation:

    • R2=0.95R² = 0.95 means 95% of the variance in job satisfaction is explained by the model.

    • A high R² suggests that the predictors have a strong explanatory power.

  • Caution: A high R² does not necessarily mean a good predictive model if overfitting occurs.

3. Adjusted R² = 0.95

  • Definition: Adjusts R² for the number of predictors to prevent overfitting.

  • Why is it important?

    • Unlike R², Adjusted R² only increases if new predictors significantly improve the model.

  • Here: Since R² and Adjusted R² are equal (0.95), it suggests that both predictors are useful and the model is not overfitting.

4. AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) = 166.66

  • Definition: A metric used for comparing models, balancing fit and complexity.

  • Interpretation:

    • Lower AIC values indicate a better model.

    • AIC is only useful for comparing models, not as an absolute measure of fit.

  • Here: Since we see only one model, we would need to compare it to another model with different predictors to determine if it is optimal.

5. BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) = 172.27

  • Definition: Similar to AIC but penalizes complexity more.

  • Interpretation:

    • Lower BIC = Better model fit.

    • More conservative than AIC in penalizing unnecessary predictors.

  • Here: Like AIC, it would need to be compared with other models to determine the best choice.

6. RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) = 3.41

  • Definition: Measures the average prediction error of the model.

  • Interpretation:

    • Lower RMSE = Better predictive accuracy.

    • It is measured in the same units as job_satisfaction, making it easier to interpret.

  • Here: An RMSE of 3.41 means that the average deviation between the predicted and actual job satisfaction values is 3.41 units.

2. Overall Model Test

Metric Value Interpretation
F-statistic 273.93 Tests whether at least one predictor significantly explains job satisfaction.
df1 (Degrees of Freedom, Numerator) 2 Number of predictors.
df2 (Degrees of Freedom, Denominator) 27 Number of observations minus predictors.
p-value < 0.0001 Indicates that the model is highly significant overall.

Interpretation of F-Test

  • The F-statistic (273.93) tests if the predictors explain a significant portion of job satisfaction.

  • p < 0.0001, so the model is highly statistically significant.

  • This confirms that at least one predictor (salary or age) significantly affects job satisfaction.

Final Conclusion

  1. Model Fit is Excellent:

    • R² = 0.95 and Adjusted R² = 0.95 confirm that the model explains 95% of the variance in job satisfaction.

  2. Predictive Performance:

    • RMSE = 3.41 suggests the model’s average prediction error is low.

  3. Model Comparison Metrics:

    • AIC (166.66) and BIC (172.27) indicate a good trade-off between complexity and fit, but require comparison with other models.

  4. Model is Statistically Significant:

    • F-test (273.93, p < 0.0001) confirms that at least one predictor significantly impacts job satisfaction.

Step 8. Assumption Checks

Check the assumptions of the regression model. Click on the Assumption Checks bar and select all options except for plots.

Interpretation of Assumption Checks in Jamovi Regression Output

Assumption checks in multiple linear regression ensure the validity and reliability of the model. In this Jamovi output, several assumption tests are performed, including normality, heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, and multicollinearity. Below is a detailed explanation of each test and its interpretation.

1. Cook’s Distance (Influence of Individual Observations)

Statistic Mean Median SD Min Max
Cook’s Distance 0.10 0.01 0.34 0.00 1.86

Interpretation:

  • Cook’s Distance measures how influential each data point is on the regression model.

  • Guideline:

    • Values greater than 1 indicate potentially influential observations.

    • Max = 1.86 suggests that at least one observation might have a high influence on the model.

  • Next Step: Check residual plots or remove influential observations to see how the model changes.

2. Normality Tests (Assumption: Residuals Should Be Normally Distributed)

Test Statistic p-value
Shapiro-Wilk 0.87 0.0014
Kolmogorov-Smirnov 0.17 0.3440
Anderson-Darling 1.21 0.0031

Interpretation:

  • The null hypothesis (H₀) for normality tests: Residuals are normally distributed.

  • p < 0.05 → Rejects H₀, meaning residuals are not normally distributed.

  • Shapiro-Wilk (p = 0.0014) and Anderson-Darling (p = 0.0031) suggest violation of normality.

  • Kolmogorov-Smirnov (p = 0.3440) does not reject normality.

  • Next Step:

    • Check residual Q-Q plots.

    • If normality is violated, consider log transformation or robust regression.

3. Heteroskedasticity Tests (Assumption: Homoscedasticity – Constant Variance of Errors)

Test Statistic p-value
Breusch-Pagan 10.81 0.0045
Goldfeld-Quandt 0.03 1.0000
Harrison-McCabe 0.75 0.9800

Interpretation:

  • Breusch-Pagan (p = 0.0045) rejects homoscedasticity, indicating heteroskedasticity (non-constant variance).

  • Goldfeld-Quandt (p = 1.0000) and Harrison-McCabe (p = 0.9800) suggest homoscedasticity.

  • Conflicting results, but since Breusch-Pagan is significant, heteroskedasticity might be an issue.

  • Next Step:

    • Use robust standard errors or transform dependent variable.

4. Durbin-Watson Test for Autocorrelation (Assumption: Residuals Are Independent)

Statistic DW Value p-value
Durbin-Watson 0.63 < 0.0001

Interpretation:

  • The null hypothesis (H₀): No autocorrelation in residuals.

  • DW Value = 0.63 → Suggests positive autocorrelation (ideal range: 1.5 to 2.5).

  • p < 0.0001, meaning strong evidence of autocorrelation.

  • Next Step:

    • Consider adding lag variables or generalized least squares (GLS) regression.

5. Collinearity Statistics (Assumption: No Multicollinearity)

Predictor VIF (Variance Inflation Factor) Tolerance
Salary 1.09 0.92
Age 1.09 0.92

Interpretation:

  • VIF < 10 and Tolerance > 0.1 → No multicollinearity.

  • Both salary and age have VIF = 1.09, meaning no problematic collinearity.

  • Next Step: No action needed.

Final Summary & Action Plan

Assumption Test Results Issue Detected? Action Plan
Influential Observations Cook’s Distance max = 1.86 Possible Check residuals and consider removing outliers.
Normality of Residuals Shapiro-Wilk (p = 0.0014), Anderson-Darling (p = 0.0031) Violated Check Q-Q plot, consider transformations.
Homoscedasticity (Equal Variance of Residuals) Breusch-Pagan (p = 0.0045) Violated Use robust standard errors or transformations.
Autocorrelation of Residuals Durbin-Watson = 0.63 (p < 0.0001) Violated (Positive Autocorrelation) Consider GLS regression or adding lagged variables.
Multicollinearity VIF < 10, Tolerance > 0.1 No issue No action needed.

Conclusion

  • The model has strong collinearity control but fails normality, heteroskedasticity, and autocorrelation checks.

  • Key concerns:

    1. Heteroskedasticity detected → Apply robust standard errors.

    2. Autocorrelation detected → Use Generalized Least Squares (GLS).

    3. Non-normal residuals → Transform dependent variable or use non-parametric regression.

Worked Example 2

In many cases, it is not easy to select the explanatory variables that best explain the dependent variable from the many possible explanatory variables. Let’s look at such an example where we collected data from 33 athletes. These are decathletes, we recorded their results in all 10 events at a given competition, and the total scores are also included.

We would like to understand the result achieved in the 400, how it may depend on the results achieved in other events?

Step 1. Import database

Open the reg_decathlon.sav file in jamovi.

Step 2. Multiple Linear Regression

Perform a multivariate linear regression analysis with the 400-meter result as the dependent variable and the results of the other sports as the independent variables which are:

  • m100 - 100 meters
  • long_jump - long jump
  • shot_put - shot put
  • high_jump - high jump
  • hurdles110 - 110 meters hurdles
  • discus_throw - discus throw
  • pole_vault - pole vault
  • javelin_throw - javelin throw
  • m1500 - 1500 meters

Interpretation of Independent Variables in the Regression Output

The image shows a multiple linear regression analysis where the dependent variable (m400) is predicted using several independent variables (covariates). Below, I provide an interpretation of each independent variable based on the regression coefficients.

1. Understanding the Regression Coefficients Table

Predictor (Independent Variable) Estimate (β) SE (Standard Error) t-value p-value Interpretation
Intercept 13.83 11.24 1.23 0.2311 The predicted value of m400 when all predictors are zero (not meaningful in this context).
m100 (100m sprint) 1.22 0.72 1.68 0.1056 Not statistically significant (p>0.05p > 0.05). Suggests a positive relationship with m400.
long_jump (Long jump) -0.24 0.55 -0.43 0.6706 Not significant (p>0.05p > 0.05). Weak negative impact on m400.
shot_put (Shot put) 0.34 0.20 1.68 0.1057 Not significant (p>0.05p > 0.05). Small positive influence on m400.
high_jump (High jump) 1.69 1.45 1.16 0.2577 Not significant (p>0.05p > 0.05). Weak positive relationship.
hurdles110 (110m hurdles) 0.72 0.37 1.92 0.0673 Close to significance (p=0.0673p = 0.0673), possibly a weak predictor.
discus_throw (Discus throw) -0.09 0.06 -1.49 0.1494 Not significant (p>0.05p > 0.05). Small negative influence.
pole_vault (Pole vault) -0.40 0.48 -0.84 0.4108 Not significant (p>0.05p > 0.05). Negative influence.
javelin_throw (Javelin throw) 0.01 0.03 0.25 0.8047 Not significant (p>0.05p > 0.05). Practically no effect.
m1500 (1500m run) 0.04 0.01 3.24 0.0036 Statistically significant (p<0.05p < 0.05), meaning it has a strong positive impact on m400.

2. Key Observations

  1. Significant Predictor:

    • m1500 (1500m run, p=0.0036p = 0.0036): The only statistically significant predictor. A one-unit increase in m1500 leads to a 0.04 increase in m400.

  2. Close to Significance:

    • hurdles110 (110m hurdles, p=0.0673p = 0.0673): Almost significant; it might contribute to predicting m400.

  3. Non-Significant Predictors:

-   All other variables **do not significantly predict `m400`**, as their **p-values are greater than 0.05**.

-   This means events like `m100`, `long_jump`, `shot_put`, and `pole_vault` do **not strongly influence** `m400`.

Step 3. A minimal model

In the previous step, we saw that the 1500-meter run (m1500) is the only statistically significant predictor for the 400-meter run (m400). Now, we will create a minimal model that includes only this variable.

Evaluation of the Independent Variable (m1500) and Comparison to the Full Model

1. Understanding the Changes in the Model

In this reduced model, only one independent variable (m1500) is used to predict m400, whereas in the previous full model, multiple predictors (e.g., m100, long_jump, shot_put, etc.) were included.

2. Evaluating the Current Model with m1500 as the Only Predictor

Metric Value (Current Model: Only m1500) Value (Previous Full Model) Change
R (Multiple Correlation Coefficient) 0.59 0.83 Decreased significantly
R² (Coefficient of Determination) 0.34 0.69 Dropped by half
Significant Predictor m1500 (p = 0.0003) Only m1500 was significant in the full model Same conclusion
Key Observations:

  • R² dropped from 0.69 to 0.34, meaning that the model now explains only 34% of the variance in m400 instead of 69% in the full model.

  • R decreased from 0.83 to 0.59, indicating a weaker overall relationship between the predictor and the dependent variable.

  • The p-value for m1500 remains highly significant (p = 0.0003), confirming that it is still a key predictor.

3. Interpretation of the Independent Variable (m1500)

Predictor Estimate (β) SE (Standard Error) t-value p-value Interpretation
m1500 0.05 0.01 4.04 0.0003 Statistically significant predictor. A one-unit increase in m1500 leads to a 0.05 increase in m400, holding other variables constant.

Conclusion: m1500 remains an important predictor, but it alone does not explain the variability in m400 as well as the full model did.

4. Comparison: Why Did the Explanatory Power Drop?

  1. Many relevant predictors were removed
-   The **full model had multiple predictors**, which together explained **69%** of the variation in `m400`.

-   The **reduced model only has `m1500`**, which explains **only 34%** of the variation.
  1. Multicollinearity may have been present in the full model
-   Some predictors in the full model may have been highly correlated, inflating R².

-   Removing them reduced redundancy, but also lowered explanatory power.
  1. Other events contribute to m400 performance
-   `m100`, `hurdles110`, or other sprint-related events might also play a role.

-   This model **ignores those contributions**, leading to a lower R².

5. Which Model is Better?

  • If the goal is prediction accuracy, the full model is better (R² = 0.69).

  • If the goal is simplicity and significance, the reduced model is better (m1500 is the only significant predictor).

  • The best approach is to balance complexity and fit, potentially using stepwise regression or AIC/BIC-based model selection.

Final Takeaway:

  • The full model explained more variance, but included many non-significant predictors.

  • The reduced model is more interpretable, but loses predictive power.

  • A better solution: Keep m1500 and reconsider adding one or two additional predictors that significantly improve R².

Step 4. Optimal model

Finding the Optimal Model in Linear Regression: A Step-by-Step Explanation

Finding the optimal linear regression model means selecting the best combination of independent variables that provide the most accurate, interpretable, and generalizable predictions for the dependent variable while avoiding overfitting and underfitting. Below is a structured explanation of the key principles and steps involved in model optimization.

1. Criteria for an Optimal Linear Regression Model

An optimal model should:

  1. Maximize explanatory power → A high R2R^2 and Adjusted R2R^2 while ensuring meaningful relationships.

  2. Minimize complexity → Avoid unnecessary predictors that do not add significant value.

  3. Improve prediction accuracy → Low RMSE and valid out-of-sample predictions.

  4. Avoid overfitting → The model should generalize well to new data.

  5. Avoid underfitting → The model should capture the essential relationships.

  6. Meet all assumptions → Linear regression assumptions (normality, homoscedasticity, independence, no multicollinearity) should hold.

2. Steps to Identify the Optimal Model: Hierarchical regression

Hierarchical regression is exactly the same as multiple regression but now we have multiple models or blocks. You can specify hierarchical regression using the Model Builder drop-down menu in jamovi. In addition, using the Model Fit drop-down menu you should check AIC and BIC in addition to the previously selected options.

Start a new Linear regression anyalysis and add the all the variables to the model. Then create 3 blocks:

  • Block 1 (for running events): m100, m1500, hurdles110
  • Block 2 (for jumping events): long_jump, high_jump, pole_vault
  • Block 3 (for other events): shot_put, discus_throw, javelin_throw

Select all metrics in the Model Fit drop-down menu.

Interpretation of the Three Models in the Image

The image presents the results of a hierarchical multiple regression analysis in Jamovi, where different predictors are added in sequential blocks to explain the dependent variable m400 (400m performance). Below, I provide a step-by-step comparison of the three models based on model fit statistics and predictor significance.

1. Model Comparison Table
Model R R² Adjusted R² AIC BIC RMSE F-statistic df1 df2 p-value
Model 1 0.78 0.61 0.57 75.70 83.19 0.65 15.35 3 29 <0.0001
Model 2 0.79 0.63 0.54 80.30 92.28 0.64 7.37 6 26 0.0001
Model 3 0.83 0.69 0.57 86.07 97.12 0.59 5.63 9 23 0.0004
Key Observations

  • R (Multiple Correlation Coefficient):

    • Increases from 0.78 (Model 1) to 0.83 (Model 3) → The added predictors improve the model’s overall correlation with m400.

  • R² (Coefficient of Determination):

    • Increases from 0.61 to 0.69, meaning that Model 3 explains 69% of the variance in m400, whereas Model 1 explains 61%.

  • Adjusted R²:

    • Fluctuates, reaching 0.57 in Model 3, meaning the new variables do not substantially improve the model beyond Model 1.

  • AIC/BIC (Model Selection Criteria):

    • Both AIC and BIC increase from Model 1 to Model 3, indicating that while Model 3 has a higher R², it also introduces more complexity without clear improvement.

  • RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error):

    • Decreases from 0.65 to 0.59, meaning Model 3 has slightly better predictive accuracy.
Conclusion from Model Fit Metrics:

  • Model 3 has the highest R² but also the highest complexity (AIC/BIC penalties).

  • Model 1 is the most efficient in terms of simplicity and performance.

  • Adding extra predictors in Model 2 and 3 only marginally improves model fit.

2. Model Comparison Table (ΔR² and Significance Tests)

Comparison ΔR² F-statistic df1 df2 p-value
Model 1 vs. Model 2 0.02 0.38 3 26 0.7713
Model 2 vs. Model 3 0.06 1.43 3 23 0.2597
Key Observations

  • ΔR² (Change in R²) is small when moving from Model 1 to Model 2 (0.02) and Model 2 to Model 3 (0.06), meaning the additional predictors do not substantially improve model performance.

  • p-values in both comparisons (> 0.05) indicate that the added variables in Model 2 and Model 3 do not significantly improve the model fit.

Conclusion from Model Comparisons:

  • Adding predictors in Model 2 and Model 3 does not significantly improve explanatory power.

  • Model 1 is the most parsimonious and should be preferred.

Final Decision:

Model 1 is the best model because it explains most of the variance while remaining simple and interpretable.

Step 5. Final model

In the previous step, we found that the best model is the one that includes only the running events (m100, m1500, hurdles110). Now, we will create a final model that includes only those variables that are statistically significant.

Create a new Linear regression analysis and add the running events to the model. We need 3 blocks again:

  • Block 1: m1500
  • Block 2: m100
  • Block 3: hurdles110

Analysis of the Three Models in the Image

The image presents results from a hierarchical multiple regression analysis, where predictors are added in sequential blocks to explain the dependent variable m400 (400m event performance). Below, I will analyze and compare the three models based on model fit statistics and predictor significance.

1. Model Comparison Table

2. Interpretation of Model Fit Metrics

  • R (Multiple Correlation Coefficient):

    • Increases from 0.59 (Model 1) to 0.78 (Model 3) → As more predictors are added, the model’s overall correlation with m400 improves.

  • R² (Coefficient of Determination):

    • Increases from 0.34 to 0.61, meaning that Model 3 explains 61% of the variance in m400, compared to 34% in Model 1.

  • Adjusted R²:

    • Also increases from 0.32 (Model 1) to 0.57 (Model 3) → This indicates that adding more predictors improved the model, though not as dramatically as raw R².

  • AIC/BIC (Model Selection Criteria):

    • Both AIC and BIC decrease from Model 1 to Model 3, indicating that Model 3 is preferred in terms of model fit while considering complexity.

  • RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error):

-   **Decreases from 0.85 to 0.65**, meaning Model 3 has better predictive accuracy than Model 1.

Conclusion from Model Fit Metrics:

  • Model 3 has the highest explanatory power (R² = 0.61) and lowest RMSE, making it the best model in terms of predictive accuracy.

  • Adding predictors significantly improved the model from Model 1 to Model 3.

3. Model Comparisons (ΔR² and Significance Tests)

Comparison ΔR² F-statistic df1 df2 p-value
Model 1 vs. Model 2 0.22 15.15 1 30 0.0005
Model 2 vs. Model 3 0.05 3.66 1 29 0.0655
Key Observations
